title: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Cors
description: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) support for ASP.NET Core APIs.

data.text: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a mechanism that allows restricted resources on a web page to be requested from another domain. Microsoft.AspNetCore.Cors provides middleware for enabling CORS in ASP.NET Core.

data.title: Enabling CORS

terms.definition: A set of rules that define which origins can access resources.
An OPTIONS request sent by the browser to check if the actual request is safe.

data.title: Security
data.text: Never use `AllowAnyOrigin()` with `AllowCredentials()` - browsers will block it.
Why Preflight Exists and How to Answer It

The browser blocks a cross-origin JavaScript request unless the server opts in. For a non-simple request — a custom header, a `PUT`, or a JSON content type — it first sends an `OPTIONS` preflight asking which methods and headers are allowed. The server must answer that preflight correctly or the real request never leaves the browser.

data.title: A named CORS policy
AllowAnyOrigin and AllowCredentials cannot coexist
data.text: The browser rejects a response that allows credentials with a wildcard origin, and .NET throws at startup if you configure it. You must name the exact origins when credentials are involved. Also remember that the middleware order matters: `UseCors` after `UseRouting` and before the endpoints so the preflight is handled before authentication rejects it.

data.title: Key Takeaways
data.takeaway: CORS is essential for enabling communication between your frontend and API.
